'''''Cephalanthera rubra''''', known as '''red helleborine''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is an [[orchid]] found in [[Europe]], [[North Africa]] and southwest [[Asia]]. Although reasonably common in parts of its range, this [[Cephalanthera]] has always been one of the rarest orchids in [[Great Britain|Britain]].

==Description== 
Each flowering shoot reaches 20–70 cm height. The shoots grow from a creeping rhizome. The stem is smooth at the base and densely covered with short glandular hairs higher up. The shoots have between 2 and 8 lanceolate leaves which range in size from 5 to 14 cm long and from 1 to 3 cm wide. Each shoot may carry up to 20 flowers, which may be pink to red or rarely white. They are up to 5 cm wide. The petals are curved and lanceolate. Flowers are produced from May to July.<ref>[https://www.first-nature.com/flowers/cephalanthera-rubra.php First Nature - Cephalanthera rubra]</ref> It is known to sometimes go many years without flowering. Chromosomes 2n=36

Not to be confused with ''[[Epipactis atrorubens]]'' (dark red helleborine).

[[File:Cephalanthera_rubra_flower_150604.jpg|thumb|Close up image of the flower.]]

==Distribution and habitat==
The red helleborine is found throughout most of [[Europe]], east to the [[Urals]] and as far as 60 degrees north. It is however rare in [[Great Britain|Britain]], the [[Low Countries]] and western [[France]]. It also occurs in [[Morocco]], [[Algeria]] and [[Tunisia]] and in various parts of southern [[Asia]] as far east as [[Iran]].<ref>{{cite book | last=Harrap | first=Anne and Simon | title=Orchids of Britain and Ireland: a Field and Site Guide | publisher=A&C Black | year=2005 | pages=134–40 | isbn=0-7136-6956-X }}</ref><ref name="WCSP">[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=36673 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=cephalanthera+rubra Altervista Flora Italiana, Cefalantera rossa, Red Helleborine, ''Cephalanthera rubra'' ]</ref>

Found in light, dry forest, particularly among [[beech]] trees, [[pine]]s and [[spruces]]. It grows to an altitude of {{cvt|2600|m}}, especially on calcareous soils with a pH between 5.9–8.2. Flower colour is an indicator of the soil qualities, with darker blooms on more calcareous ground.

Red helleborine is a very rare plant in [[Great Britain|Britain]]. It is found only at the following sites:
* [[Workmans Wood, Sheepscombe|Workmans Wood]], [[Sheepscombe]], [[Gloucestershire]]<ref name="NBN">[https://data.nbn.org.uk/imt/?mode=SPECIES&species=NHMSYS0000457046 Species distribution map for Cephalanthera rubra] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161104003204/https://data.nbn.org.uk/imt/?mode=SPECIES&species=NHMSYS0000457046 |date=2016-11-04 }}, [[NBN Gateway]], retrieved 25 February 2010</ref><ref>Kitchen, Clare, Mark A. R. Kitchen and Ian Carle (2008) Stephen Bishop's New Flora of Gloucestershire Part 2: the distribution maps ''The Gloucestershire Naturalist'' No. 14 Gloucestershire Naturalists ' Society, page 232</ref><ref>Fisher, John (1991) ''A colour guide to rare wild flowers'' {{ISBN|0-09-470780-4}} Constable books, London</ref>
* [[Hawkley Warren]], [[Hampshire]],<ref name="NBN"/> where it was first found in 1986.<ref>Rose, F. and A. Brewis (1988) [http://www.watsonia.org.uk/Wats17p163.pdf Short notes: ''Cephalanthera rubra'' in Hampshire] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726103308/http://www.watsonia.org.uk/Wats17p163.pdf |date=July 26, 2011 }} ''[[Watsonia (journal)|Watsonia]]'' 17: 176-77</ref>
* [[Windsor Hill SSSI]], a woodland just to the east of [[Princes Risborough]] in the [[Chilterns]], [[Buckinghamshire]]<ref name="NBN"/><ref>Ratcliffe, D. A. (1977) ''A Nature Conservation Review Volume 2. Site Accounts'' p. 53 {{ISBN|0-521-21403-3}}</ref>

During the 19th and early 20th centuries, the species was recorded from single sites in [[Somerset]], [[Sussex]] and [[Kent]], and a second [[Hampshire]] site (in the upper [[Test Valley]]). The species was also recorded at additional [[Gloucestershire]] sites (including Stanley Wood, [[King's Stanley]], now a [[Woodland Trust]] woodland, and [[Uley]]<ref>See letter of J.B.H. Baker (grandson of William  William Lloyd Baker (1752–1830), the first to identify it locally, by its [[Basionym|basionym]]  ''Serapias rubra'', L. 1767) from [[Hardwicke Court]], Gloucester, dated 14 September 1864, in ''The Journal of Botany, British and Foreign'', vol. 2, 1864, p. 346.</ref>), and persisted at some of these into the 1970s. It became a protected species in the UK in 1975 under the Conservation of Wild Creatures and Wild Plants Act.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.caithness.org/caithnessfieldclub/bulletins/1975/october/conservation.htm|title = Caithness CWS - Caithness Field Club - Annual Bulletins - 1975 - October - Conservation}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Cephalanthera rubra'' is thought to be mainly pollinated by [[Diptera|flies]], although often self-pollination is triggered by rainfall.<ref name="researchgate.net">[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/280532300_Beobachtungen_von_Miarus_campanulae_als_Bestauber_von_Cephalanthera_rubra Beobachtung von Miarus campanulae als Bestäuber von Cephalanthera rubra]</ref> Pollination may also be carried out by ''[[Chelostoma]]'' bee (''[[Chelostoma campanularum]]''?) and the [[weevil]] ''[[Miarus campanulae]]'', both of which are thought to mistake the flowers for ''[[Campanula persicifolia]]'', a wildflower found on mountains in continental Europe. It is theorised that ''C. rubra'' mimics ''C. persicifolia'' to increase pollination early in the year.<ref name="researchgate.net"/>

As the flowers are frequently visited by flies, [[Thomisus|crab spiders]] have been observed hunting in them.<ref name="researchgate.net"/>

''C. rubra'' forms a [[mycorrhizal fungi|mycorrhizal]] relationship with species in the genera ''[[Leptodontidium]]'', ''[[Phialophora]]'' and ''[[Tomentella]]''. This enables it to access soil nutrients which would otherwise be unavailable.<ref>[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/8395420_Changing_partners_in_the_dark_Isotopic_and_molecular_evidence_of_ectomycorrhizal_liaisons_between_forest_orchids_and_trees Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Changing Partners in the Dark: Isotopic and Molecular Evidence of Ectomycorrhizal Liaisons between Forest Orchids and Trees]</ref>

==Etymology==
''[[Cephalanthera]]'' comes from the [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] κεφαλή ανθηρός, meaning "head flowering", thought to be a reference to the protruding position of the [[anthers]]. The species epithet ''rubra'' comes from the [[Latin]] for red, referring to the colour of the flowers. The Latin binomial was chosen by a French botanist named Professor [[Louis Claude Marie Richard]].

"Helleborine" may refer to deer using the orchid for food (many conservationists have noted that helleborine orchids are grazed by deer <ref>[https://www.plantlife.org.uk/application/files/4914/7913/4059/Epipactis_youngiana_species_dossier.pdf Plantlife - Epipactis youngiana]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/wfsoc/wfs_reports/2001/2001_watlington_hill_11_july_report.htm |title=Wildflower Society Online Report |access-date=2018-12-06 |archive-date=2018-12-06 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181206192538/https://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/wfsoc/wfs_reports/2001/2001_watlington_hill_11_july_report.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[http://kammekat.tripod.com/ceplongifoliaen.htm Finnish Orchids]</ref>). Alternatively it may denote that the plants are similar to [[hellebores]] (a group of species in the family [[Ranunculaceae]]). "Hellebore" comes from the Greek "álkē" and "bora", translating as "fawn" and "food of beasts".<ref>[https://www.dictionary.com/browse/hellebore Dictionary.com]</ref>

In [[German language|German]], ''Cephalanthera'' are referred to as Waldvöglein, meaning little birds of the wood, a reference to the winged appearance of the flowers.

==Monitoring==
The protection of red helleborine should aim to preserve specific forest biotopes for this species. During monitoring of this species, the number of shoots (vegetative and generative), leaf area and number of fruits are recorded. It is recommended to collect metrological data (sum of precipitation and air temperature), as well as data on shading, vegetation at the site, the presence of bells (Campanula sp.) in the vicinity and the abundance of dead wood.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lewoń |first1=Radoslaw |last2=Romanski |first2=Maciej |title=New locations, distribution and protection of the red helleborine Cephalanthera rubra (L.) Rich. (Orchidaceae) in the Augustów Primeval Forest (NE Poland) |journal=Leśne Prace Badawcze (Forest Research Papers) |lang=pl |date=November 2023 |volume=83 |url=https://www.ibles.pl/lesne-prace-badawcze-artykul/nowe-stanowiska-rozmieszczenie-i-ochrona-bulawnika-czerwonego-cephalanthera-rubra-l-rich-orchidaceae-w-puszczy-augustowskiej-ne-polska/ |pages=46–50 |doi=10.48538/lpb-2023-0004 |access-date=20 October 2024 }}</ref>
